title: Why, despite midterms, a reset in US-global diplomacy could take a long time
text:
Why, despite midterms, a reset in US-global diplomacy could take a long time
A Democratic Congress could help to change the way the U.S. interacts with other parts of the world.
At a market on the east side of Paris, Jérémie Graine hands out flyers for the left-wing French presidential candidate Raphaël Glucksmann.
Mr. Graine is deeply involved in his own nation’s politics but also has a keen eye on a much wider issue: Europe’s relationship with the United States, and how that has changed under President Donald Trump’s administration.
“I don’t feel any damage to our relationships with Americans, the people,” he says. “It’s Trump who reinforces a bad image of the U.S. I’m worried that, despite the midterm results, he’ll push whatever he needs to push, by force.”
The United States’ relationship with Europe and other parts of the world has shifted considerably during the Trump presidency. Following the midterm elections and a Democratic majority in Congress, analysts are considering what it will take to restore America’s reputation abroad.
Fellow canvasser Suzanne Amicel agrees. “We want to have a good relationship with the United States,” she says. “Like before.”
Ms. Amicel and Mr. Graine were pleased with the results of the U.S. midterms, which they see as a rebuke of President Trump’s policies. But they also say there is much more to be done to repair the damage to transatlantic relations over the last two years.
Rebuilding U.S.-European ties is something that many are thinking about after the Democratic Party’s electoral success. How much a Democratic Congress can accomplish will be a key question during the remainder of Mr. Trump’s time in office.
Need for predictability and consistency
The world has watched with alarm as this president launched trade wars with allies, dismantled America’s most vaunted lever of soft power, and raced into a war with Iran that has left parts of the world feeling less safe and reeling from high energy prices.
America’s global reputation is so low that a recent Pew Research poll found China is viewed more positively abroad than the United States.
The road to repairing America’s image internationally will be a long one, likely stretching on for years, analysts say.
“Losing as badly as the Republicans did is significant. It suggests the emperor has no clothes,” says Daniel Drezner, professor of international politics at the Fletcher School at Tufts University.
But, he says, “It’s tricky because the president still has significant power.”
A Democratic majority in Congress may be able to leverage its power of the purse by defunding the unpopular war with Iran and calling hearings to hold the Trump administration accountable. It could also try to introduce new legislation signaling change, such as sanctions on Russia.
Democratic Rep. Gregory Meeks, the likely incoming chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has pointed to a need for increased oversight of foreign policy amid corruption allegations, and sent letters to agencies warning them not to destroy or conceal records to impede congressional inquires and investigations.
“We need to provide our allies with the predictability and consistency upon which deterrence rests,” says Torrey Taussig, director of the Atlantic Council’s Transatlantic Security Initiative. Restoring that will be essential to rebuilding trust, she argues.
Following the landslide defeat for the Republicans in Congress, Mr. Trump’s hands are largely tied domestically. So, he may do what other presidents have done before him: double down on foreign policy, the purview of the executive, including making high-profile trips abroad. He is currently on an Asian tour featuring a planned summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
There is precedent for a new U.S. president turning the tides of international opinion. Following America’s unpopular war with Iraq, the panacea was enthusiasm for a new American leader, the internationally engaged President Barack Obama.
But Dafna Rand, a senior fellow at The Brookings Institution, believes that this time the situation is very different. “The Trump tariffs are a wholesale rejection of long-term U.S. alliances in Europe and in Canada,” she says.
“Rebuilding these U.S. alliances will face a much longer and harder road to recovery,” she adds. “The Democratic Congress believes in alliances, but it also wants to manage expectations about going back to a pre-Trump order as it will be much harder to reset the clock.”
Future of soft power
Under the Trump administration the U.S. Agency for International Development has been dismantled. Since its founding by President John F. Kennedy, USAID has funded development overseas to combat starvation, disease outbreaks, and poverty – all with the goal of building American security and alliances through doing good. Previous Republican and Democratic administrations viewed the agency as the jewel of U.S. soft power.
“Development will have to be completely reimagined,” says Dr. Taussig, a former director for European affairs on the National Security Council. “It won’t be possible to just turn the clock backwards. It’s going to be more about reimagining than restoring, by repairing trust and predictability.”
Need to collaborate
Historically, one of America’s longest and closest alliances has been with neighboring Canada. But the current situation is at such a low point that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described the changing relationship as a “rupture, not a transition.” He was speaking following the trade dispute between the two countries and what Canadians view as a fundamental threat to the sovereignty of their nation with President Trump’s calls to make Canada the 51st U.S. state.
“Canadians have taken this very personally,” says Erin O’Toole, a former leader of the opposition in the Canadian Parliament. “This administration has made a lot of Canadians feel ... disrespected.”
A so-called “Trump slump” is being felt in some U.S. states as many Canadians have stopped traveling to them in response.
Citing a long history of economic integration and cooperation, specifically in the auto industry, energy sector, and in agriculture, Mr. O’Toole says, “I’d love to see us back to coordinating so we can make North American manufacturing more productive and bring costs down.”
“We need to collaborate, not trade threats,” he says.
